technique.how: Patient fixes gaze on your nose; hold the head with both hands and deliver a small (10-20 degree), rapid, unpredictable horizontal head turn to each side, watching the eyes as the head stops. A corrective ('catch-up') saccade back to your nose after the turn indicates a deficient vestibulo-ocular reflex on that side (abnormal = peripheral); eyes that stay locked on target = normal.
technique.prerequisites: Only interpretable in acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus); the patient must be able to fixate. Warn the patient and check cervical range of motion first.
technique.contraindications: Cervical spine instability or acute neck injury, known carotid/vertebral dissection, severe cervical spondylosis.

interpretation.positive_finding: Abnormal test (catch-up saccade) supports a peripheral vestibular lesion (vestibular neuritis) on the side toward which the head was turned; in Kattah 2009 an abnormal h-HIT was present in 100% of peripheral cases.
interpretation.negative_finding: A NORMAL head impulse test in a patient with acute vestibular syndrome is the dangerous result: it suggests a central (stroke) cause - present in about 80% of central AVS (pooled) and 93% in Kattah 2009 (NLR 0.07).
interpretation.pitfalls: The direction of inference is inverted relative to most tests (normal = worrying); AICA strokes involving the labyrinth give a falsely 'peripheral' abnormal HIT (sensitivity only 36% for AICA strokes), so a positive HIT must be combined with nystagmus and skew (HINTS/HINTS+). Small saccades are easily missed by untrained examiners, and the test is meaningless without spontaneous nystagmus.
interpretation.changes_what: Normal HIT in AVS: treat as central; stroke pathway/MRI. Abnormal HIT: supports neuritis only if nystagmus is unidirectional and no skew; otherwise still image.

estimates.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome - normal horizontal head impulse test
estimates.population: Pooled AVS cohorts (10 study cohorts, n=800; hHIT assessed in 422 central and 378 peripheral patients)
estimates.reference_standard: Delayed MRI-DWI for peripheral cases; confirmatory neuroimaging for stroke
estimates.quote: Sensitivity for detecting a central cause of AVS was highest for a normal hHIT (79.9% [95% CI 72.2-87.5])
estimates.location: Results, 'Diagnostic accuracy of bedside examination findings' (Ann Neurol 2023;94:295; PMC10524166); supplementary Table 2

estimates.target_condition: AICA-territory stroke in AVS - normal hHIT alone
estimates.population: AICA stroke subgroup of pooled AVS cohorts
estimates.quote: AICA strokes were missed more frequently when applying the hHIT alone (sensitivity=36.0% [20.2-55.5])
estimates.location: Results, 'Diagnostic accuracy in AVS stratified by stroke location', Table 4 (Ann Neurol 2023;94:295; PMC10524166)

estimates.target_condition: Central cause of acute vertigo/dizziness - head impulse test (normal = central)
estimates.population: ED patients with acute vertigo or dizziness; 17 studies, 1366 patients (not restricted to AVS)
estimates.quote: head impulse test (HIT)-17 studies, 1366 patients, sensitivity 76.8% (64.4%-85.8%, low) and specificity 89.1% (95% CI 75.8%-95.6%, moderate)

estimates.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome - h-HIT normal or untestable
estimates.population: 101 consecutive high-risk AVS patients (25 peripheral, 76 central); neuro-ophthalmologist examiner
estimates.reference_standard: MRI (or CT) for stroke; normal MRI plus clinical follow-up for peripheral
estimates.location: Table 1 (PAVS n=25 vs CAVS n=76), Stroke 2009;40:3504 (PMC4593511)

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Not valid outside acute vestibular syndrome (no spontaneous nystagmus, episodic or positional vertigo), in patients who cannot fixate, or with cervical instability/dissection. Do not use HIT alone to rule out stroke.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: A normal head impulse in a patient with continuous vertigo and nystagmus is a stroke warning even with normal CT; an abnormal HIT does not exclude AICA infarction, especially with new hearing loss.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Accuracy depends on examiner expertise: bedside HIT sensitivity for central lesions was as low as 58% in one non-expert cohort (Machner, cited in Ann Neurol 2023); video-HIT meta-analysis reports sens 84%/spec 85% (PMID 40447837, not cited as estimate).

extraction_notes: Direction of inference: here 'positive for central' = NORMAL HIT, so pooled sensitivity refers to the proportion of central AVS with a normal HIT. Ann Neurol 2023 (PMC full text) gives pooled sensitivity in the Results text but specificity only in supplementary Table 2 (not viewable) - left null. GRACE-3 (abstract) pools a broader ED vertigo/dizziness population (not AVS-only), so it is reported as a separate estimate. Kattah 2009 Table 1 values read from PMC full text; specificity 100% = 0/25 peripheral. Tarnutzer 2011 CMAJ anchor: abstract-only PMC deposit, cited without numbers.
